note: Theory that is heard, not recited: tap the three roots on the staff and hear the chord built on each, follow the chords in order, then in a new order without looking. Chords are chord tokens, named in the player's key, and the first section counts them the long way ("the 1st chord of the key, built on" its note) before any step asks for a number. The key is moves (any key), and the last line says what stays the same in another key. Works for any instrument, or none.

exercise.title: The 1st, 4th and 5th chords in {{=key}}, by ear
exercise.why: Each chord is built on one note of the scale, so once you hear the root move between the 1st, 4th and 5th notes, you can tell which chord is playing.

cells.text:
The staff below shows the {{=key}} major scale: tap a note to hear it. Tap the three ringed notes, {{1}}, {{4}} and {{5}}.
A chord can be built on each of them. {{chord:I}} is the 1st chord of the key, built on {{1}}. {{chord:IV}} is the 4th chord, built on {{4}}. {{chord:V}} is the 5th chord, built on {{5}}.
Press Play under each chord box below, from left to right, to hear the three chords.

Press Play below to start the backing track: {{chord:I}}, {{chord:IV}}, {{chord:V}} and back to {{chord:I}}, one bar each. Say the number of each chord as it arrives, 1, 4 or 5, with the lit box to help.
Practice until you hear a change coming before the box lights.

Press Play below to start the backing track: the same three chords in a new order. Look away from the screen, say the number of each chord, and look back to check.
If you can't tell which chord is playing, wait for {{chord:I}}: it sounds like home, and you can follow the order again from there.
{{?key}}In another key the three chords have other names, and each still sounds the same against the home note: the 1st chord like home, the 4th and 5th chords away from it.
